transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-04-22 15:00 PDT | Duration: 58 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (CTO - StratusBio), Liam O'Connor (Infra Lead), Maya Rivera (Security), Ethan Park (SRE)

Auto-generated sections:
Topics: multi-region routing, failover playbooks, capacity & warm pools, KV cache replication, batching/quantization effects, VPC/on-prem peering, KMS replication
Action items: see metadata

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: all right everybody thanks for joining, we'll kick off. this is Jordan from Redwood, i think we've got, uh, Priya from the SE team as well. can everyone hear me?
[00:10] Aisha Khan: yeah good to go, thanks Jordan. we've been looking forward to this one — multi-region routing is a big piece for us.
[00:20] Priya Nair: hi all. quick agenda: we'll walk through policy routing options, capacity considerations, KV cache consistency, and then DR/failover playbooks. happy to dive into the infra specifics when you want.
[00:35] Liam O'Connor: perfect — context quick: StratusBio runs mostly in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 today, planning ap-southeast-1 in Q3. primary concern is patient-data latency for internal UX and also HIPAA-like constraints for certain workloads.
[00:50] Maya Rivera: and from security side we need KMS/HSM keys in customer control, audit logs, and SSO/SAML integration — plus data residency controls.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: understood. first, policy routing overview — Redwood supports routing by latency, cost, region, and customer tier. you can define a primary region and a fallback chain; we also support weighted split traffic for canaries.
[01:25] Priya Nair: it's important to note there are two patterns: active-active with local caches, and active-passive with prefix routing. active-active reduces cross-region latency but introduces cache sync complexity.
[01:40] Ethan Park: when you say cache sync, do you mean KV cache replication? how eventual is it?
[01:45] Priya Nair: yeah so our KV cache is per-region by default — low-latency local reads. replication is async; we don't do synchronous global KV replication because that kills request latency. instead we keep a coherent prefix invalidation approach and TTLs. that means in failover you might see cold starts for some prefixes.
[02:10] Aisha Khan: hmm that could be rough for real-time UX. what's the typical cold-start delta?
[02:15] Priya Nair: typical cold-start adds 30-120ms for KV miss scenarios on top of generation latency, depending on model and whether the sequence is cached. for long-context workloads the impact is higher because kv warm-up is more costly.
[02:35] Liam O'Connor: and batching — if traffic shifts regionally, does batching behavior change? our throughput budgets assume large batches for cost-efficiency.
[02:45] Priya Nair: yes, batching is workload-dependent. when requests are routed across regions you may see smaller effective batch sizes per GPU, which raises per-token cost and can affect tail latency. Redwood's routing tries to preserve batching affinity by routing stickiness (session-level) when configured.
[03:05] Jordan Lee: we can set session affinity with a configurable window, e.g., 30s to 5min, to maximize batching while still allowing failover. tradeoff is slightly longer recovery if a region goes down.
[03:20] Maya Rivera: for compliance we need to ensure if data is not allowed to leave region X, routing won't send it elsewhere even as fallback. can we do policy-based geo-blocking?
[03:30] Priya Nair: yes — per-route policies can include geo constraints and model-level residency. fallback only occurs to allowed regions; we also support private deployments (Redwood Private) where the control plane is isolated and you can keep all inference inside your VPC/on-prem.
[03:50] Ethan Park: for Private deployments, does Redwood still control routing decisions or does that run inside our VPC?
[03:55] Jordan Lee: control plane can be customer-managed in the Private option — routing logic runs in your environment, and you can use our orchestration components but keep decisioning behind your firewall.
[04:10] Aisha Khan: let's dig into failover playbooks — what are the recommended steps when a region degrades vs. total outage?
[04:18] Priya Nair: recommended: 1) detect via health checks and SLO breaches, 2) degrade non-critical routes (low-tier) first, 3) move critical traffic using prioritized fallback chain, 4) warm up instances in fallback region with prefetched hot prefixes and synthetic traffic, 5) increase batch windows temporarily to catch up.
[04:40] Liam O'Connor: about warming — how do you pre-populate KV cache in failover region without leaking data across regions? encryption concerns too.
[04:50] Priya Nair: good point. for customer-managed KMS, keys are region-scoped; we do not replicate plaintext. We support encrypted cache snapshots that can be transferred via encrypted channels and only decrypted with customer KMS in target region. There is an operational step where you approve the snapshot restore.
[05:10] Maya Rivera: that sounds better than automatic replication — but how long does snapshot restore take?
[05:15] Priya Nair: typical restore for hot prefixes is seconds to a couple minutes depending on size; full cache rebuild could be tens of minutes. hence the playbook focuses on hot prefix prioritization.
[05:30] Jordan Lee: also note model artifacts and quantized weights — if you have region-local model variants (quantized to int8 or q4), we ensure compatibility and provide fallback model variants that are smaller but faster to instantiate. tradeoff is some quality delta.
[05:50] Aisha Khan: can you do dynamic re-quantization during failover? like spin a lower-precision model to warm faster?
[05:55] Priya Nair: yes, we often recommend a two-tier fallback: primary full-precision model in each region plus a lighter quantized fallback that can be instantiated very quickly. you can route degraded traffic to the quantized model while the full one warms.
[06:10] Ethan Park: curious about network constraints — we have strict peering rules and only allow cross-region traffic via Transit Gateway; limited NAT bandwidth in some regions. how does Redwood's routing respect egress limits?
[06:22] Jordan Lee: routing policies can include egress capacity constraints — you define region capacity and burst budgets; the router will respect those budgets and only failover if target region has capacity. This avoids saturating peering links.
[06:36] Liam O'Connor: who owns the capacity calculation? do we pre-commit vGPU counts with Redwood Dedicated?
[06:42] Jordan Lee: for Dedicated, you pre-commit capacity and we reserve warm pools. for Hosted routing we apply quota and throttling; we can also reserve burst capacity across regions with committed blocks.
[06:55] Maya Rivera: audit logs — we need to see every routing decision, who triggered failover, and the signed policy. are those logs available in the Private control plane?
[07:05] Priya Nair: yes, Private exposes full audit logs, and Hosted can stream audit events to your SIEM. logs include policy evaluation traces, routing decisions, health events, and model variant swaps.
[07:20] Aisha Khan: ok re: latency SLOs — what's realistic for us-east to fallback in eu-west for 1k tokens?
[07:27] Priya Nair: if you go cross-region, you'll add one-way network latency (60-120ms typical between us-east and eu-west) plus model runtime. total tail latency could rise by 150-300ms depending on model size and batching. that's why we prioritize regional fallbacks and warm pools.
[07:50] Ethan Park: given those deltas, we might want to limit fallback to warm-critical APIs only. can we define per-route SLO enforcement?
[07:58] Jordan Lee: absolutely — you can attach SLO policies per route and have automatic fallback only when SLOs are met or as an emergency override.
[08:10] Liam O'Connor: in a DR scenario, do you recommend switching DNS or using an edge routing approach?
[08:18] Priya Nair: we prefer edge routing with health checks rather than DNS TTL flips. DNS changes are slow; our router at the edge can failover per-request. for Private deployments you can run an internal edge with the same logic.
[08:35] Aisha Khan: what's the cost impact of keeping warm pools in three regions? we have budget constraints.
[08:42] Jordan Lee: warm pools add fixed cost; we typically size them for hot requests. cost optimization strategies: 1) keep minimal warm pool and rely on quantized fallbacks, 2) use burst blocks (pay for short-term capacity), 3) prioritize which routes get warm pools. Redwood Optimize can analyze traffic and recommend minimal warm sizes.
[09:05] Maya Rivera: one more security question: KMS keys and cross-region access — if we keep keys in us-east only, can you do crypto ops in eu-west?
[09:12] Priya Nair: cryptographic ops must use region-local keys; you can replicate keys to other regions under your HSM policy, or you can keep keys region-scoped and use encrypted snapshots as mentioned. we do not move unencrypted data across regions.
[09:30] Ethan Park: OK can we walk through a concrete example — region failover from us-east -> eu-west under heavy load?
[09:35] Priya Nair: sure. detect: edge health checks show 5xx rate spike and latency breach. router begins shedding low-tier traffic, then pins critical sessions to fallback eu-west. we spin up warm GPU instances in eu-west from the warm pool or burst cap, restore hot prefixes via encrypted snapshot, route a growing % of traffic over a 30s-2min ramp while monitoring SLOs. once stable, we fully cutover and leave monitoring and audit trails.
[10:05] Aisha Khan: what about database calls and downstream side-effects? are there recommended patterns to avoid split-brain?
[10:12] Priya Nair: avoid stateful side effects in the model runtime, push stateful writes to region-aware services. For cross-region requests that might hit different backends, use idempotency tokens and versioned data writes. part of the DR playbook is identifying stateful vs stateless routes.
[10:30] Liam O'Connor: any gotchas with Kubernetes or on-prem infra? we run a hybrid k8s cluster in some regions.
[10:36] Priya Nair: Redwood runtime can run in k8s or on dedicated nodes. k8s autoscaling and GPU scheduling can add cold start delays; for critical routes we recommend pinned nodes or node pools with pre-warmed containers. for on-prem, network egress constraints and private registries are common friction points.
[10:58] Jordan Lee: quick interjection — also watch out for model quantization differences across hardware — some GPUs perform int8 faster; others have better fp16 kernels. our kernel selection tries to pick the closest compatible variant, but we document perf deltas.
[11:14] Ethan Park: ok let's talk benchmarks — what do you need from us to run a 3-region bench?
[11:20] Priya Nair: config: representative prompt distribution, token lengths, concurrency profile, session affinity settings, and allowed regions. also network peering constraints and any max egress limits. we'll provide a default benchmarking harness and a results spreadsheet.
[11:36] Jordan Lee: action: Priya will send the benchmark config and harness; Liam to provide network diagram and egress limits.
[11:45] Aisha Khan: timeline — we want a pilot in prod-like environment by end of May. realistic?
[11:52] Jordan Lee: yes for a limited pilot with dedicated warm pools and a single critical route we can aim for end of May. full three-region production may take longer.
[12:00] Maya Rivera: procurement/security wants to see SOC2 + data processing addendum.
[12:05] Jordan Lee: will send security pack. we have SOC2 Type II and can provide architecture diagrams and DPA template.
[12:12] Ethan Park: are there metrics we should track during the DR test?
[12:15] Priya Nair: yes: request latency p50/p95/p99 per route, KV hit ratio, warm-pool utilization, model load times, batch size distribution, and egress bandwidth. also track error budget burn.
[12:32] Liam O'Connor: one more thing — do you support canarying across regions for gradual rollouts?
[12:37] Priya Nair: yes, weighted traffic split across regions with canary analysis and automatic rollback rules. you can route N% to fallback region for validation.
[12:48] Jordan Lee: ok let's open for any outstanding questions.
[12:52] Aisha Khan: regarding warm-pool cost allocation — can we get per-route cost estimates?
[12:58] Jordan Lee: yes we'll include per-route cost estimate in the pilot pricing.
[13:03] Maya Rivera: on the KMS side, we also need to verify HSM compatibility for FIPS requirements.
[13:08] Priya Nair: we support HSM-backed keys and can integrate with customer HSMs in Private. we'll share the HSM integration notes.
[13:20] Ethan Park: if a region goes full down for an hour, what's the expected customer-visible impact assuming warm pools are sized conservatively?
[13:28] Priya Nair: you'd see increased tail latency for some sessions, some prefix cold starts, and possibly increased cost due to smaller batching. but we design the playbook to keep critical routes within SLO by using warm pools and quantized fallbacks.
[13:46] Jordan Lee: recap before we close: Redwood to share playbook, benchmark harness, security pack; StratusBio to share network diagram and compliance list; schedule DR tabletop for early May.
[14:01] Aisha Khan: that summary works. thanks everyone.
[14:06] Jordan Lee: thanks — action items in the notes. we'll follow up by email with the links.
[14:12] (meeting ends)
notes: Redwood recommends hot-prefix snapshot restores for failover to minimize cold-starts
Quantized fallback models are recommended for faster instantiation with acceptable quality tradeoffs
Policy routing supports geo-blocking and per-route SLO-driven failover
Private control plane option available for customer-managed routing decisions and audit logs
